questions.title: Duration of stored ATP for muscle contraction
questions.question: The total quantity of ATP stored within the cells of the body is sufficient for contraction for a maximum of how many seconds?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stored ATP pool is smaller than this, sufficient for only a few seconds of contraction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This overstates the tiny directly-stored ATP pool; sustained contraction beyond a few seconds relies on regeneration (via creatine phosphate, then glycolysis/oxidative phosphorylation), not on stored ATP itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The cell's directly stored ATP is enough to fuel contraction for only about 4 seconds; this is precisely why the ATP-ADP cycle must turn over extremely fast and why creatine phosphate exists as an immediate secondary buffer to regenerate ATP as it is spent. This is why regenerating ATP, not simply storing more of it, is the cell's real energetic strategy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This overstates the stored ATP pool by a wide margin.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cell's directly stored ATP lasts only a few seconds of contraction, motivating the need for creatine phosphate as an immediate buffer.

questions.title: Well-fed state muscle fuel uptake
questions.question: During the well-fed state, muscles take up ___ to replenish glycogen and ___ amino acids to synthesise proteins.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fatty acids are the preferred fuel of the early-fasting state, not the substrate muscle takes up to replenish glycogen in the well-fed state.
explanations.B: Correct. In the well-fed, insulin-driven state, muscle takes up circulating glucose to replenish its glycogen store, alongside taking up amino acids to synthesise contractile and structural protein. This matches the general well-fed shift toward anabolism seen across the body's tissues.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acetyl-CoA is an intracellular metabolic intermediate, not a circulating fuel that muscle takes up from the blood to build glycogen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyruvate is likewise an intracellular glycolytic intermediate, not the substrate muscle imports from the circulation to replenish glycogen.

questions.learning_objective: State that well-fed muscle takes up glucose to replenish glycogen.

questions.title: Early fasting state muscle fuel
questions.question: In the early fasting state, resting muscle uses ___ as fuel.

explanations.A: Correct. In the early fasting state, resting muscle preferentially oxidises circulating fatty acids as fuel, sparing glucose for tissues that depend obligately on it (e.g. the brain and red cells) before more significant protein breakdown becomes necessary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucose is spared for obligate glucose-using tissues during fasting, not preferentially burned by resting muscle at this stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amino-acid-derived fuel (from protein breakdown) becomes more significant only in prolonged fasting, not in the early fasting state resting muscle is described in here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acetone is a minor, largely exhaled ketone-body byproduct, not resting muscle's preferred early-fasting fuel.

questions.learning_objective: State that early-fasting resting muscle preferentially burns fatty acids, sparing glucose.

questions.title: Duration creatine phosphate can support exercise
questions.question: The concentration of creatine phosphate ('phosphocreatine') in muscle can support exercise for a maximum of how many seconds?

explanations.A: Incorrect. This overstates how long the muscle's creatine phosphate store alone can sustain maximal exercise before other systems (anaerobic glycolysis) must take over.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This understates the duration on this exam's printed figure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This understates the duration by a wider margin.
explanations.D: Correct. Muscle's creatine phosphate store can support near-maximal exercise for up to about 30 seconds -- the phosphagen (ATP-CP) system is the fastest but most limited energy source, bridging the gap between the few seconds of stored ATP and the several-minutes capacity of anaerobic glycolysis. This roughly 30-second window is what the ATP-CP system buys before glycolysis must take over.

questions.learning_objective: State the approximate duration (about 30 seconds) that the creatine phosphate store can support near-maximal exercise.

questions.title: Oxidative system's fuel sources
questions.question: In muscle, the oxidative system depends on the supply of reduced equivalents from:

options.A: Complete oxidation of glucose in the TCA cycle

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Complete glucose oxidation via the TCA cycle does supply reduced equivalents, but it is not the only source feeding the oxidative system.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. Fatty acid oxidation likewise supplies reduced equivalents but is not the sole source.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. Ketone-body oxidation contributes reduced equivalents too, but again is not exclusive.
explanations.D: Correct. The mitochondrial oxidative (aerobic) system draws its reduced equivalents (NADH, FADH2) from all three fuel classes together -- complete oxidation of glucose through the TCA cycle, beta-oxidation of fatty acids, and oxidation of ketone bodies -- which is exactly why the aerobic system can sustain far longer, more efficient ATP regeneration than the anaerobic glycolysis or phosphagen systems alone. No single fuel class alone accounts for the oxidative system's full capacity.

questions.learning_objective: State that the aerobic oxidative system draws reduced equivalents from glucose, fatty acid and ketone-body oxidation together, not any single fuel alone.

questions.title: Organ where creatine synthesis starts
questions.question: Creatine starts its synthesis in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brain takes up finished creatine via a transporter; it is not the organ where synthesis begins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The intestine plays no role in creatine's biosynthetic pathway.
explanations.C: Correct. Creatine synthesis begins in the kidney, where AGAT transfers the amidino group of arginine to glycine, forming guanidinoacetate. The two-organ division of labour is a frequently tested sequencing fact.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The liver performs the second step of synthesis (GAMT methylating guanidinoacetate to creatine), not the first.

questions.learning_objective: Name the kidney as the organ where creatine synthesis begins.

questions.title: Amino acids creatine is synthesised from
questions.question: Creatine is synthesised from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alanine is not one of creatine's three source amino acids; arginine is required for the first (kidney) step.
explanations.B: Correct. Creatine synthesis draws on three amino acids: glycine and arginine combine at the kidney step (AGAT) to form guanidinoacetate, and methionine (as SAM) supplies the methyl group at the liver step (GAMT) to complete creatine. Each of the three amino acids plays a distinct, non-interchangeable role in the pathway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glutamate is not one of creatine's source amino acids; glycine is required for the kidney step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alanine does not supply the methyl group -- methionine (via SAM) does; alanine plays no role in creatine synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: Name glycine, arginine and methionine as creatine's three source amino acids.

questions.title: Elevated plasma creatinine indicates impaired organ
questions.question: Elevation of creatinine level in plasma indicates impaired function of the:

explanations.A: Correct. Creatinine is cleared from plasma almost entirely by glomerular filtration, so a rising plasma creatinine reflects falling glomerular filtration rate -- impaired kidney (renal) function -- which is exactly why serum creatinine is used clinically as an index of renal function. This is the same logic that makes creatinine clearance a practical bedside estimate of GFR.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The liver's function is assessed by other markers (e.g. transaminases, bilirubin, albumin); creatinine is not a liver-function marker.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Brain function is not assessed by plasma creatinine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intestinal function is not assessed by plasma creatinine.

questions.learning_objective: State that elevated plasma creatinine indicates impaired kidney (glomerular filtration) function.

questions.title: Tissue specificity of creatine kinase 2 (CK-MB)
questions.question: Creatine kinase 2 (CK-MB) is relatively specific for the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. CK-BB (CK1), not CK-MB, predominates in brain.
explanations.B: Correct. Creatine kinase exists as tissue-specific isoenzymes built from M and B subunits; CK-MB (CK2) is relatively specific to cardiac muscle, which is why its rise in plasma is used clinically as a marker of myocardial injury. Recognising the isoenzyme's tissue origin is what makes it clinically useful as a marker.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CK-MM (CK3), not CK-MB, predominates in skeletal muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. None of the three classic creatine kinase isoenzymes is specific to intestine.

questions.learning_objective: Name CK-MB as the creatine kinase isoenzyme relatively specific to cardiac muscle.

questions.title: Clinical scenario with raised CK-MB
questions.question: Creatine kinase 2 (CK-MB) level is increased in plasma in the case of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Muscle dystrophy classically raises total CK (largely the CK-MM/skeletal-muscle isoenzyme), not specifically CK-MB.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Brain damage would be reflected by the brain-specific isoenzyme CK-BB, not CK-MB.
explanations.C: Correct. Because CK-MB is relatively specific to cardiac muscle, myocardial injury (as in myocardial infarction) releases it into the circulation, making a rise in plasma CK-MB a classic (if now largely superseded by troponin) marker of MI. This tissue specificity is exactly why CK-MB, rather than total CK, was historically favoured for diagnosing MI.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lung disease is not associated with a rise in CK-MB.

questions.learning_objective: Apply CK-MB's cardiac specificity to identify myocardial infarction as the scenario that raises it.

questions.title: Fuel source in the absence of oxygen
questions.question: Which of the following is a fuel source of energy in the absence of oxygen?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fatty acid oxidation is a strictly mitochondrial, oxygen-dependent process and cannot proceed in the absence of oxygen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ketone-body oxidation is likewise mitochondrial and oxygen-dependent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatine (phosphate) is a rapid ATP buffer via creatine kinase, not itself a fuel that is metabolised for energy the way glucose or fatty acids are.
explanations.D: Correct. Under anaerobic conditions, muscle can only regenerate ATP by breaking down glycogen/glucose via anaerobic glycolysis, since it does not require oxygen -- fatty acid and ketone-body oxidation are both unavailable without it. Every other listed option requires oxygen and is therefore unavailable under truly anaerobic conditions.

questions.learning_objective: State that glycogen/glucose, via anaerobic glycolysis, is the only fuel usable in the absence of oxygen.

questions.title: What the amount of muscle creatine phosphate depends on
questions.question: The amount of creatine phosphate in muscle depends on:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Muscle activity governs how fast creatine phosphate is used up and regenerated during exercise, not the baseline total amount stored.
explanations.B: Correct. The total amount of creatine phosphate a muscle holds scales with its mass ('bulk') -- more muscle tissue means more creatine phosphate stored overall, the same logic by which total-body creatinine production tracks muscle mass. This is the same principle that links muscle mass to a person's baseline creatinine production.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibre type influences fatigue resistance and oxidative capacity more than the baseline creatine phosphate content specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Anatomical site is not the determining factor for creatine phosphate content; muscle mass is.

questions.learning_objective: State that a muscle's creatine phosphate content scales with its mass.

questions.title: Organ needing active methionine for creatine synthesis
questions.question: Synthesis of creatine needs the active form of methionine in the:

explanations.A: Correct. GAMT, the second creatine-synthesis enzyme, acts in the liver and requires the active form of methionine -- S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) -- as its methyl donor to convert guanidinoacetate to creatine. This localises the rate-limiting methylation chemistry to a single organ, distinct from the kidney's earlier step.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscle takes up finished creatine via a transporter; it is not the site requiring SAM for synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Brain likewise takes up finished creatine; it is not the site of the SAM-dependent methylation step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The kidney performs the first (AGAT) step, which uses arginine and glycine, not SAM.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The heart does not perform the SAM-dependent methylation step of creatine synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: Name the liver as the organ where SAM (active methionine) is used to complete creatine synthesis.

questions.title: Enzyme used in creatine synthesis in the kidney
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes is used in creatine synthesis in the kidney?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Guanidoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) acts in the liver, the second step, not the kidney.
explanations.B: Correct. Arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) acts in the kidney, the first step of creatine synthesis, transferring the amidino group of arginine to glycine to form guanidinoacetate. This kidney-specific step is the first of the pathway's two organ-divided reactions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatine kinase phosphorylates finished creatine to creatine phosphate in muscle/brain, a downstream step, not the kidney synthesis step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adenylate kinase interconverts adenine nucleotides (2 ADP <-> ATP + AMP), an unrelated enzyme.

questions.learning_objective: Name AGAT as the enzyme used in the kidney step of creatine synthesis.

questions.title: Enzyme used in creatine synthesis in the liver
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes is used in creatine synthesis in the liver?

explanations.A: Correct. Guanidoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) acts in the liver, the second step of creatine synthesis, methylating guanidinoacetate using SAM to produce creatine. This liver-specific step is the second of the pathway's two organ-divided reactions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) acts in the kidney, the first step, not the liver.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatine kinase acts downstream in muscle/brain, phosphorylating creatine to creatine phosphate, not in the liver synthesis step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adenylate kinase is an unrelated nucleotide-interconversion enzyme, not part of creatine synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: Name GAMT as the enzyme used in the liver step of creatine synthesis.

questions.title: What SAM donates in creatine synthesis
questions.question: S-Adenosyl Methionine (SAM) is important in creatine synthesis to donate a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The guanido (amidino) group comes from arginine at the earlier kidney (AGAT) step, not from SAM.
explanations.B: Incorrect. SAM does not donate acetate; that is not part of creatine synthesis chemistry.
explanations.C: Correct. SAM is the universal methyl donor used by GAMT to methylate guanidinoacetate, producing creatine and releasing S-adenosylhomocysteine. No other cofactor in this pathway supplies a methyl group.
explanations.D: Incorrect. SAM does not donate a hydroxyl group; hydroxyl-group chemistry belongs to the vitamin-C-dependent collagen hydroxylases or the vitamin D hydroxylases, not to creatine synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that SAM donates a methyl group in creatine synthesis.

questions.title: Earliest energy system for a 100m sprint
questions.question: The earliest energy system which provides ATP for a 100-metre sprinter (9 seconds) is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ketone-body oxidation is a slow, oxygen-dependent process, far too slow to be the earliest source for an explosive few-second sprint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anaerobic glycolysis takes over as the phosphagen system depletes, over the following tens of seconds to a couple of minutes -- it is the second, not the earliest, system engaged.
explanations.C: Correct. For an explosive, very short effort like a 9-second 100-metre sprint, the phosphagen (ATP-CP) system -- stored ATP plus creatine phosphate rapidly regenerating it via creatine kinase -- is the earliest and fastest available energy source, engaged within the first couple of seconds of the sprint. As the sprint continues past its first few seconds, anaerobic glycolysis then takes over the load.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aerobic glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation are far too slow to power the initial seconds of an explosive sprint; they dominate only in longer, sustained efforts.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fatty acid oxidation is a slow, oxygen-dependent process suited to prolonged low-to-moderate intensity exercise, not an explosive sprint's opening seconds.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the phosphagen (creatine phosphate) system as the earliest energy source for a short, explosive sprint.

questions.title: Order of enzymes in creatine metabolism
questions.question: Arrange the following enzymes in creatine metabolism: 1) Guanidoacetate methyltransferase; 2) Arginine, glycine amidinotransferase; 3) Creatine kinase; 4) Non-enzymatic conversion to creatinine. Which is the correct order?

explanations.A: Correct. Creatine metabolism runs: AGAT (2, kidney) forms guanidinoacetate from arginine and glycine -> GAMT (1, liver) methylates it to creatine -> creatine kinase (3, muscle/brain) phosphorylates creatine to creatine phosphate -> creatine (and creatine phosphate) spontaneously, non-enzymatically converts to creatinine (4) at a rate proportional to muscle mass. Getting this four-step order right ties together synthesis, storage and clearance in a single sequence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This places GAMT (1, the liver step) before AGAT (2, the kidney step), but AGAT must act first to make the guanidinoacetate that GAMT then methylates.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This places creatine kinase and non-enzymatic conversion to creatinine before either synthesis enzyme has acted, which is impossible -- creatine must first be made before it can be phosphorylated or break down to creatinine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This runs the entire sequence backwards, starting from creatinine formation and ending at the first synthesis step.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This places creatine kinase (3) before GAMT (1), but creatine kinase can only phosphorylate creatine after GAMT has actually produced it.

questions.learning_objective: Sequence creatine metabolism from AGAT through GAMT and creatine kinase to non-enzymatic creatinine formation.

questions.title: Decreased creatinine -- what it indicates
questions.question: A decreased amount of creatinine in plasma and urine indicates:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Impaired kidney function (reduced filtration) raises, not lowers, plasma creatinine, since less is cleared.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Brain function is not reflected by creatinine levels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because creatinine production is proportional to muscle mass, increased muscle mass would raise, not lower, creatinine production -- the opposite of a decreased level.
explanations.D: Correct. Because creatinine forms at a rate proportional to muscle mass, a loss of muscle mass or function -- as in muscle dystrophy and weakness -- reduces total creatinine production, lowering both plasma and urinary creatinine even though kidney function itself may be normal. This is why a 'normal-looking' creatinine can be misleading in a patient who has already lost significant muscle mass.

questions.learning_objective: Explain a decreased creatinine as reflecting reduced muscle mass/function (e.g. dystrophy), not kidney disease.

questions.title: Normal serum creatinine in males
questions.question: The normal amount of serum creatinine in males is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This uses the wrong unit (mg/L instead of mg/dL), understating the concentration by a factor of ten.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This uses grams per decilitre, a unit far too large for creatinine's actual plasma concentration (that magnitude is closer to a protein concentration such as albumin).
explanations.C: Incorrect. This likewise uses grams per litre, again far too large a unit for creatinine.
explanations.D: Correct. Normal serum creatinine in males is approximately 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL, the standard clinical reference range used to assess renal function alongside creatinine clearance. Values outside this range prompt further evaluation of renal function or muscle mass.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal serum creatinine reference range in males, 0.6-1.2 mg/dL.

questions.title: Diagram: amino acid combining with glycine at the kidney step
questions.question: In the diagram of creatine synthesis, which amino acid combines with glycine at the kidney step to begin creatine synthesis?

explanations.A: Correct. Arginine is the amino acid that combines with glycine at the kidney step: AGAT transfers arginine's amidino group onto glycine, releasing ornithine and forming guanidinoacetate, the diagram's first labelled reaction. This kidney-step reaction is the pathway's committed first step.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Methionine (as SAM) acts later, at the liver step, donating a methyl group -- it is not the amino acid combining with glycine at the kidney step.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lysine plays no role in this reaction; it is instead a substrate of the unrelated collagen-hydroxylation and cross-linking pathway.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alanine plays no role in creatine synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: Name arginine as the amino acid that combines with glycine at the kidney step of creatine synthesis.

questions.title: Diagram: the other amino acid at the kidney step
questions.question: In the diagram of creatine synthesis, which amino acid is combined with arginine at the kidney step to form guanidinoacetate?

explanations.B: Incorrect. Serine plays no role in creatine synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proline plays no role in creatine synthesis; it belongs instead to the collagen hydroxylation pathway.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Threonine plays no role in creatine synthesis.

questions.question: In the diagram of creatine synthesis, which enzyme catalyses the kidney step that forms guanidinoacetate?

explanations.A: Correct. AGAT is the diagram's third labelled component, the enzyme that catalyses the kidney step transferring arginine's amidino group to glycine to form guanidinoacetate. explanations.D: Incorrect. Xanthine oxidase belongs to the unrelated purine catabolism pathway.

questions.title: Diagram: the methyl donor at the liver step
questions.question: In the diagram of creatine synthesis, which compound donates the methyl group at the liver step that converts guanidinoacetate to creatine?

explanations.A: Correct. S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the diagram's fourth labelled component, is the amino-acid-derived methyl donor GAMT uses to methylate guanidinoacetate into creatine, releasing S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in the process. SAM's role here parallels its role as the universal methyl donor in other biosynthetic pathways.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Folate carries one-carbon units in other pathways (e.g. purine/pyrimidine synthesis, homocysteine remethylation) but is not the methyl donor GAMT uses directly in this reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase (regenerating methionine/SAM) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, but it is not itself the methyl donor in the GAMT reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acetyl-CoA donates acetyl, not methyl, groups, and plays no role in creatine synthesis.

questions.title: Diagram: the liver-step enzyme
questions.question: In the diagram of creatine synthesis, which enzyme catalyses the liver step that converts guanidinoacetate to creatine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. AGAT acts at the earlier kidney step, forming guanidinoacetate from arginine and glycine, not at the liver step.
explanations.B: Correct. GAMT is the diagram's fifth labelled component, the liver enzyme that methylates guanidinoacetate (using SAM) to complete creatine synthesis. This liver-step enzyme completes the two-organ division of labour that defines creatine synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatine kinase acts downstream in muscle/brain, phosphorylating finished creatine to creatine phosphate, not at the liver synthesis step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adenylate kinase is an unrelated nucleotide-interconversion enzyme.
